clinicalPearls: Properdin deficiency is the principal X-linked complement deficiency, so it predominantly affects males.
It markedly increases susceptibility to fulminant meningococcal disease, which can be rapidly fatal even at first presentation.
Meningococcal infection in properdin deficiency often presents acutely and with a high case-fatality rate rather than the recurrent pattern seen in terminal-pathway defects.
Properdin is the only known positive regulator of complement, stabilising the alternative-pathway C3 convertase.
The AH50 alternative-pathway assay is abnormal while the CH50 classical-pathway assay is typically preserved.
A specific low or absent properdin level confirms the diagnosis after alternative-pathway dysfunction is shown.
Meningococcal vaccination, including conjugate quadrivalent and serogroup B vaccines, and family screening are essential.
Patient and family education about seeking urgent care for febrile illness can be life-saving.
reference.pathophysiology: Properdin (factor P) is the sole positive regulator of the complement system: it binds and stabilises the alternative-pathway C3 convertase, prolonging its half-life and amplifying complement deposition on microbial surfaces. In its absence the alternative pathway cannot be sustained, so amplification of C3b deposition and downstream membrane attack complex formation on Neisseria is impaired. This leaves the host unable to mount rapid complement-mediated killing of meningococci, producing a striking vulnerability to fulminant meningococcal sepsis. Because the classical and lectin pathways remain functional, susceptibility is largely confined to neisserial organisms, and the disease is inherited in an X-linked pattern, so affected individuals are typically male.
additionalDifferentials: Terminal complement component deficiencies (C5 to C9)
Factor D or other alternative-pathway defects
additionalInvestigations: Genetic testing of the CFP gene
Cultures and PCR during acute infection to identify serogroup
X-linked family screening and carrier assessment
redFlags: Fever with headache, neck stiffness or a non-blanching rash
Rapidly progressive meningococcaemia or septic shock
Any febrile illness in a known properdin-deficient individual
Family history of fatal meningococcal disease
reference.prognosis: The main hazard is fulminant meningococcal disease with a high case-fatality if not treated immediately; with vaccination, education and prompt antibiotics the outlook is greatly improved. Because episodes can be overwhelming at first presentation, prevention and rapid response are paramount.
pitfalls: Overlooking an X-linked complement defect in a male with severe meningococcal disease.
Relying on a normal CH50 to exclude complement deficiency when the defect is in the alternative pathway.
Failing to provide serogroup B and conjugate meningococcal vaccination.
Not screening male relatives after an index case.
Underestimating how rapidly meningococcaemia can progress in these patients.
references: Middleton's Allergy: Principles and Practice, current edition
Oxford Textbook of Medicine, current edition
Reviews on complement deficiency and meningococcal susceptibility
management: Immunise fully against Neisseria meningitidis with both quadrivalent conjugate (ACWY) and serogroup B meningococcal vaccines, with boosters as advised
Educate the patient and family to seek immediate medical care for any febrile illness and, where appropriate, supply stand-by antibiotics
Treat suspected invasive meningococcal disease as an emergency with immediate parenteral third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone, fluid resuscitation and intensive care support
Consider long-term prophylactic penicillin in selected patients to reduce meningococcal risk
Screen at-risk male relatives and provide genetic counselling, as the deficiency is X-linked
Keep routine immunisations current and refer to clinical immunology for coordinated preventive care
